correctness.rationale: Kosche et al. Proposition 3.21, inspected in full text, proves that the alternating-arch word A_k maximizes the number of SAS at fixed universality index k. Their adjacent-inequality characterization specializes over {0,1} to the two updates (p,q)->(p+q,q) and (p,q)->(p,p+q). Alternating updates produce consecutive Fibonacci numbers and total F_{k+3}. For minimum length 2k, every arch is 01 or 10; sorting the two counts gives the inductive envelope (F_{i+1},F_{i+2}), and equality forces updating the smaller coordinate at each step, hence alternating blocks. The packaged verifier independently reconstructs SAS sets by direct subsequence testing for all binary words through length 12.

Neither inspected source nor targeted indexed and web searches states the binary exact value F_{k+3} or the minimum-length equality classification.

value.rationale: The primary paper highlights exponentially large SAS sets because their output size motivates compact representations and extremal analysis, but leaves its quantitative A_k count deliberately non-tight. The later tight-bounds paper still uses algorithms rather than a general closed form. The binary case is the fundamental smallest alphabet: replacing a qualitative exponential statement by the exact Fibonacci extremum supplies a sharp output-size law, and the minimum-length equality classification identifies precisely when that extremum occurs in the smallest representatives.
